#3411. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

Warning: Spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

The Hunger Games series has never been one to shy away from putting its characters through the most unimaginable horrors. But the latest movie in the franchise, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, just might take the cake. Author Suzanne Collins took the brutality in this one to a whole new (and devastating) level, putting readers through some of the darkest moments in the franchise's history. From the Capitol's calculated cruelty to the horrifying propaganda they promote, this story is a reminder of just how little control the districts held before Katniss entered the Games.

Set during the Second Quarter Quell, the latest from the Hunger Games franchise centers around one of the most brutal Games yet, with 48 tributes fighting to the death. With twice as many children thrown into the arena, the stakes are that much higher and the losses are seemingly endless. The book itself doesn't hold back from these heart wrenching losses either, going into the nitty-gritty gory details of what really went down in the arena.

While it's totally understandable that the filmmakers need to make adjustments to the story to maintain its PG-13 rating, several of the novel's more disturbing moments unfortunately didn't make the cut. One particularly disturbing moment was missing from Sunrise on the Reaping's ending, which was the grisly death of Wellie.

One of the most horrifying moments in the Sunrise on the Reaping book is when Wellie meets her demise. While the movie doesn't nearly showcase how gruesome her death is, Suzanne Collins did not hold back. During the Games, Silka, District 1's tribute, kills Wellie by cutting off her head with an axe, making it one of the most memorable and brutal deaths the series has seen so far.

The violence isn't the only part of Wellie's death that makes this moment so painful. It also reveals how ruthless Silka has become. At this point in the Games, whatever humanity Silka had left has ultimately disappeared. And all that's left is her animalistic instinct to survive, no matter what it takes. She's no longer just a tribute determined to win, she is a savage, willing to commit unimaginable acts of violence in order to win. Her transformation is so important to the story, especially in contrast to Haymitch's much more merciful attitude.

And of course, the broadcast doesn't necessarily see this death play out the way Haymitch does in the book. Wellie's death all points back to Sunrise on the Reaping's theme of how the Capitol uses propaganda to maintain their power. This death, in particular, shows the devastating consequences on the kids' psyche while they're in the Games, and the movie's choice to leave it out is all the more disappointing.

It's not particularly surprising that Sunrise on the Reaping changed the way Wellie's death is depicted in the film. Despite the already dark subject matter of the series, the films have kept a PG-13 rating, meaning that filmmakers have had to be strategic about how much graphic violence they can actually show.

These movies certainly aren't lacking in death or violence, but they often rely on quick cuts and character reactions instead of showing every brutal detail. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, SOTR director Francis Lawrence explained:

“What’s great about Suzanne’s writing is that she pulls no punches. The only thing we have to do in the movies is make them PG-13. So there's certain things she describes in the book that I could never put in the movies. There’s a character holding the head of a child at one point in the book, and that’s just not something you can do in a PG-13 movie.”

Wellie's death presents a very difficult challenge because her decapitation is much more graphic than a PG-13 audience would expect to see. Showing that death the way it's written in the book would have pushed the movie into a more restrictive place, with the risk of losing a huge part of its audience. As a result, Silka still murdered Wellie, but it is significantly less graphic.

While it's understandable that Sunrise on the Reaping couldn't recreate every gruesome detail of Wellie's death without potentially jeopardizing its PG-13 rating, that doesn't mean the filmmakers made the right decision by toning down the moment. In fact, leaving out the nature of her death takes away from one of the most disturbing turning points in the story.

Wellie's decapitation isn't just part of the story for shock value, but it's an important indicator of how high the Second Quarter Quell's stakes have become. It shows how far tributes are willing to go to survive.

More importantly, the moment says a lot about Silka and the role she has in the Sunrise on the Reaping cast. Wellie was one of the younger tributes and not particularly dangerous, so Silka didn't necessarily need to decapitate her. Wellie was never a true threat to Silka, or anybody, for that matter. But in losing this moment in the film, her transition into true savagery isn't shown.

Now, the filmmakers didn't necessarily need to show the death in every graphic detail to preserve the meaning of the scene. A longer sequence, stronger reactions from Haymitch and Silka, or more attention to the aftermath could have communicated the same horror without pushing the movie past its PG-13 rating.

Beyond changing the circumstances of Wellie's death, Sunrise on the Reaping missed the opportunity to do more with her as a character. With 48 tributes, it naturally has a lot of characters to introduce with stories to balance, but that shouldn't mean the minor characters have to fade into the background.

In the Sunrise on the Reaping novel, Wellie is a District 6 tribute and a member of Haymitch and Ampert's alliance, The Newcomers. She is also one of the kids in the arena who quickly realizes everything is poisonous. On the last day of the Games, Haymitch sticks with Wellie and hides her under a tree while he goes to locate dry kindling. In his mind, Wellie was to be the victor, and he was going to try his hardest to make that happen.

This is what makes her death even more heartbreaking. Haymitch saw Wellie as worth protecting because he thought she'd be a much better victor than himself. His choice to stay with her also shows that he genuinely believed she'd have a chance of making it out alive.

In the movie, Wellie is only seen for a couple of seconds when Haymitch offers her his lunch. Had that connection been established earlier, viewers would have had more of a reason to care about her before she died. Her relationship with Haymitch could've reinforced his arc in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping even more.

#3409. ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Officially Rebels Against Critics With Massive Audience Score

The latest installment of The Hunger Games has arrived, and audiences have spoken. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the second prequel in Suzanne Collins' popular YA dystopian franchise, and it didn't sit well with critics upon release. But what about audiences? Now that the movie has entered theaters, the viewers have spoken about their return to Panem.

Sunrise on the Reaping takes place 24 years before the events of the first Hunger Games story, during the 2nd Quarter Quell, a special Hunger Games with new rules added every 25 years to remind the districts of their defeat in the rebellion. This is the game Haymitch Abernathy participated in, now played by Joseph Zada, and the new rules for this Hunger Games were that each district would send double the number of tributes, increasing the total from 24 to 48 children in the arena.

When the critics' score came out, Sunrise on the Reaping debuted with a 74% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, and as of writing, the number has dropped to 67%. However, now that the movie has entered theaters, audiences disagree, and it sits at a 95% Verified Hot Audience Score. Audience reception was also positive on Letterboxd, with the film earning a 4.1-star rating. Collider's Victoria Luxford gave Sunrise on the Reaping an 8/10 score in her review. She praised the movie's "dark and gritty" portrayal of Collins' world but criticized the runtime, especially for those "not heavily invested" in the series.

Ever since The Hunger Games film franchise began in 2012, six films have been released: four main movies and two prequels. According to Rotten Tomatoes critics' scores, the highest-rated Hunger Games movie is the sequel, The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, with a 90% score, followed by the first Hunger Games movie at 85%. And despite Sunrise on the Reaping's low critics' score, the lowest-rated Hunger Games movie from critics is the first prequel film, The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, with a 64% rating.

Audiences, however, viewed the franchise differently: Sunrise on the Reaping is the audience's highest-rated Hunger Games movie ever, followed by Catching Fire with an 89% rating, then the first Hunger Games movie with an 81% audience score. The audience's lowest-rated installment is The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2, with an audience score of 66% on Rotten Tomatoes.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is now showing in theaters. Follow Collider for more updates.

#3408. Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’

Rian Johnson isn’t writing a Star Wars movie, but he isn’t ruling one out, either.

Responding to a question from IndieWire during an in-conversation event at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, the writer/director of “Star Wars: The Last Jedi” was clear that his next project lies elsewhere: “I’m already writing the next thing I’m going to do, and it’s not a Star Wars thing, or in that genre,” he said.

“I’m very much enjoying just making my own stuff, but I mean, if the opportunity presented itself,” Johnson said, nodding. “It’s a world I deeply love. It’s also a group of people I love.”

“I love Star Wars more now than I ever have,” he added. “And it’s exciting to me that there are a lot of different voices now taking cracks at it.” The timing is hard to ignore. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

Johnson’s remarks land just as Lucasfilm appears to be turning back toward the corner of the saga he helped shape. Polygon reported that two long-gestating features, “Star Wars: New Jedi Order” and an untitled film from Dave Filoni, are still listed as in development by Production Weekly, despite months of silence and the soft box office performance of “The Mandalorian & Grogu.”

“New Jedi Order” would theoretically bring back actress Daisy Ridley as Rey roughly 15 years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” rebuilding the Jedi Order that “The Last Jedi” so memorably called into question. Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is attached to direct, with George Nolfi now writing after earlier drafts from Damon Lindelof and Justin Britt-Gibson, and a stint by Bond 26 screenwriter Steven Knight. The film was pulled from its December 17, 2027 release date in May 2025. Meanwhile, “Star Wars: Starfighter,” the Shawn Levy-directed film starring Ryan Gosling and set five years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” remains the only Star Wars feature with a firm date: May 28, 2027.

In 2017, the year “The Last Jedi” hit theaters, Lucasfilm announced that Johnson would create a new Star Wars trilogy. Those films have yet to materialize, but Johnson had warm words for Filoni, who took on the role of Lucasfilm’s president and chief creative officer in January: “Dave Filoni I got to know while making ‘The Last Jedi’, and he’s a wonderful guy who really has the spirit of Star Wars in him,” he said. “All the Lucasfilm folks are awesome.”

Later, answering questions from the audience, Johnson described “The Last Jedi” as “the most joyful process of any movie I’ve ever made”, despite the challenge of stepping from his own original films into what he called a contested mythology.

“I’m a huge, huge fan of George Lucas, and I’ve read a lot about when he was writing the original Star Wars, how personal it was for him,” Johnson continued. “I think especially with something that has a deep cultural impact, and that belongs to everybody, that makes it even more important… to make sure it’s coming from a personal perspective and something that’s deeply on fire inside you, as opposed to thinking, ‘what’s gonna please this person and this person and this person’. That leads to homogeneity, to repeating yourself and to something that feels dead on screen.”

As a middle chapter, “The Last Jedi” drew directly on Johnson’s childhood experience of “The Empire Strikes Back,” though not as something to copy. “I didn’t want to imitate ‘The Empire Strikes Back’,” Johnson said. “What I wanted to get to was the heart of what that movie has, which is this center part of life where your job is to fail, and your job is to learn from that and to get up and keep moving forward.”

He drew a distinction between a film having a moral compass and having a moral. The compass, he said, “comes from the entire mass of every single creative decision made by the writer, or director, or whole team.”

Johnson also reflected on the only two composers he has worked with. His cousin Nathan Johnson has scored his films since the pair started making movies together at age ten: “Nathan is the first person to read the script; he’s on set for the entire shoot so it’s very much a collaboration.”

John Williams, he said, is also “a miracle of a human being”, and working with him was the opposite experience. “You give him the movie and then the first time I hear any music is when we’re on the scoring stage, and there are 200 musicians playing it.”

If Johnson does return to Star Wars, it seems he won’t be thinking about franchise strategy. “For me it’s not about thinking about IP, it’s about stories,” he said. “I deeply believe the only way to actually make a movie that matters and is worth something is to have your eyes nowhere else except on making that movie. What is the story we’re telling? Why are we telling it? Why do we care about it?”

“Outside of that bubble,” Johnson added, “I’ll leave it to the executives.”

With those executives now steering Star Wars back toward Rey and the post-“Rise of Skywalker” era, the bubble may be closer to his than it has been in years.

#3407. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3406. Wizard Of Oz Gets A Mad Max Twist In Dark New Adaptation Releasing In 3 Months

David Pepose’s comic book The O.Z. has found a home with Boom! Studios, and he explains what the series is about and how the idea came to be.

David Pepose is one of the most versatile writers in comics. Readers can see him bringing Layla El-Faouly from the MCU's Moon Knight to Marvel Comics and writing the amazing Cable: Love and Chrome. Then, he’ll turn around and give horror fans an amazing comic book like Mad Cave Studios' The Devil That Wears My Face. Among the amazing comics David Pepose has written is a bold reimagining of the classic book and movie, The Wizard of Oz, The O.Z.

The O.Z. began its push on Kickstarter, but was recently picked up by Boom! Studios. In a recent interview ScreenRant was fortunate enough to have with Pepose, he talks about what the story is about, the way it came to be, and more.

The O.Z. is one of the most creative changes to the classic book and movie. When asked about what the story is about, Pepose goes into great detail about it and why it's different from other Wizard of Oz tales.

David Pepose: THE O.Z. is like Mad Max meets The Wizard of Oz — it’s the story of Dorothy Gale’s granddaughter and namesake, who is an Iraq war veteran grappling with PTSD and disillusionment. But when our new Dorothy is caught up in a tornado, she finds herself stranded in the land of Oz — where she learns her grandmother’s adventures plunged the country into a brutal civil war. Now Dorothy must team up with the Tin Soldier, the Prince of Lions, and Jack Pumpkinhead in order to find the Silver Slippers and bring peace to the Occupied Zone… or as the locals call it, The O.Z.

Many people have brought different versions of The Wizard of Oz to various genres, but Pepose's has been the most adventurous. Considering the source material, that says a lot. When asked about that, he said, "I’ve always been a fan of mashing up different genres, so doing a fantasy war story was something I’d wanted to do early in my career." However, how he landed on The Wizard of Oz is a funny story.

Pepose: Landing on The Wizard of Oz came across as kind of a happy accident — I was typing different fantasy staples to see if anything could serve as inspiration, and my cursor froze in the middle of the word “Oz.” That had me thinking about the word Oz as an acronym, which turned into “Occupied Zone” — and that moment instantly crystallized the entire narrative for me.

When asked why he went this particular route with Dorothy, Pepose gives an interesting reason.

Pepose: Back in my days as a newspaper reporter, I’d interviewed a ton of returning veterans about their experiences coming back home, and those stories had always stuck with me — and that became the basis for Dorothy’s story in THE O.Z.

Now that The O.Z. has been picked up by Boom! Studios, the next question is whether or not the series will continue. Pepose seems hopeful that this won’t be the last comic book fans will see of the characters and this alternate reality Wizard of Oz story. However, there are some factors to consider.

Pepose: Never say never! Whether we do a sequel storyline will ultimately be determined by demand and me and Ruben Rojas’ respective schedules, but I do have a few ideas in my back pocket, which I’d actually pitched to BOOM!’s Editor-in-Chief Andy Schmidt and our O.Z. editor Gregory Hopkins. So there’s definitely room to return to the Occupied Zone if enough people demand it.

The O.Z. #1 is scheduled to be released in February 2027 by Boom! Studios.

#3405. DC’s ‘Clayface’ Officially Removed From 2,300 Theaters Ahead of Digital Release

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Nearly a month into its release, DC's Clayface has slowed down considerably. The comic book film has delivered a modest performance at the box office so far, and will soon enter the next phase of its journey when it lands on the PVOD market. The movie's box-office run was marred by the sudden announcement that DC Studios co-CEOs James Gunn and Peter Safran, who shepherded the project from its standalone origins and integrated it into the DC Universe franchise, were departing from their positions after four years. Clayface, which revolves around the iconic Batman villain, is the last film of their tenure.

The movie is only the third theatrical release of the one-year-old DC Universe, which began with Gunn's Superman reboot and continued with this summer's Supergirl. Starring David Corenswet, Superman grossed nearly $620 million worldwide against a reported budget of $225 million, which was deemed successful enough for a follow-up to be greenlit. The movie in question, Man of Tomorrow, will be released in 2027.

Earlier this year, audiences roundly rejected the Supergirl spin-off feature, starring Milly Alcock and directed by Craig Gillespie. The movie grossed $126 million worldwide against a reported budget of around $180 million. By comparison, Clayface cost around $40 million to produce, and should be able to surpass Supergirl globally this week. However, the movie has lost a significant number of theaters over the last couple of weeks and is about to lose even more.

It'll enter its fifth week of release in 1,147 theaters, down from its opening-week theater count of 3,458. Starring Tom Rhys Harries, Naomi Ackie, and Max Minghella, the movie received mostly positive reviews. It's now sitting at a "Certified Fresh" 78% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "Carving out a unique identity for itself in the DCU while closely resembling a litany of body horror classics, Clayface takes time to get going until it eventually morphs into an icky and satisfying revenge thriller."

Rather unusually for a horror movie, Clayface holds an exceptionally high "Verified Hot" 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. This indicates a bright future on digital, where it's expected to land on December 8. Although the movie didn't break out like many would've liked, it has now tripled its reported budget theatrically. This may be enough for the movie to break even, but it's a fraction of what major superhero movies are able to generate these days. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3403. Pokémon Black & White Return With Impressive Single-Screen Remaster

There have been all sorts of brilliant Pokémon games over the years, and while everyone has their own favorites, it's widely agreed upon that Black and White are some of the best releases in the series to date. In fact, the DS/3DS era as a whole was just a magical time for franchise releases more generally, and they remain popular games for fans to play in 2026.

That movement has only been furthered by the rise of PC emulation, which has become easier and considerably more competent in recent years thanks to rapid advances in technology. One of the main issues with emulating DS games is the dual screens they were originally designed for, which don't lend themselves particularly well to modern, single-monitor setups.

Happily, it seems as though those concerns are about to entirely be a thing of the past, as a new and ingenious piece of tech finally solves the issue with aplomb.

As first reported by Retro Dodo, new software has been made publically available that converts dual-screen Pokémon games into a single-screen 60FPS output. Known as Pokémon FullDex, it's available as a free download from creator mamesj's GitHub, and it already works for a ton of iconic games from the DS era.

The description for the project reads as follows:

"All your favourite Pokémon games on a PC (Windows and Linux), a Mac, a Steam Deck or other handheld PC, an Android phone, an iPhone or iPad, or a modded Nintendo Switch: one screen, widescreen, 60 fps, up to 4K on a PC and 720p on the Switch. No more squinting at two tiny stacked DS screens."

The videos posted to the page are also hugely impressive, and you'd never really know that the games weren't designed to run like that in the first place. It works far beyond Pokémon Black and White as well, with more titles on the way all the time. The full list as it stands includes:

DS: Black 2, White 2, Black, White, HeartGold, SoulSilver, Platinum, Diamond and Pearl.

GBA: Emerald, Ruby, Sapphire, FireRed, LeafGreen and Ultra Violet.

3DS (beta): Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire on Windows, Android and Switch; X, Y, Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon coming soon.

It's a hugely impressive, lightweight piece of tech, and it comes with a bunch of mod-cons like support for RetroAchievements and cheats. The only potential drawback here is that it seems as though the project was heavily assisted by Claude AI, and that comes with its own set of risks, as well as potential moral quandaries for those of us who want to push back against the increased use of AI in gaming.

As for Pokémon fans more generally, the 30th anniversary of the franchise has now largely drawn to a close, and things are expected to go a little quiet for the time being. The first games of the tenth generation (Winds and Waves) are set to be the next big stopping point on that journey, with more news expected on that in the first half of next year.

#3399. HBO's 28-Episode Dystopian Series Is So Good, Even Its Weakest Episode Beats Most Sci-Fi Shows

The weakest episode of one of HBO’s best Mystery Box shows arrived early in the three-season run of the series, but even this outing still had plenty to praise, which highlights the overall quality of the show as a whole. Mystery Box shows are somewhat infamous for their inconsistency. While early seasons of Lost include some of the most enthralling and engaging network TV moments of the 2000s, the show’s filler episodes can feel truly pointless.

Even the earliest Mystery Box shows weren’t immune to this. The best episodes of Twin Peaks were funny, scary, heartbreaking, disturbing, and beautiful, often at the same time, but anyone who has sat through the latter half of season 2 can attest to the show’s plentiful padding. Similarly, while there were mytharc episodes of the ‘90s classic The X-Files that were truly unmissable, there were plenty of other outings that made the central conspiracy more confusing, but not more interesting.

The fact that almost every Mystery Box show has at least a few duds among its great episodes makes HBO’s The Leftovers all the more impressive. Based on the novel of the same name by author Tom Perrotta, HBO’s dark mystery drama takes place after an unexplained disaster sees 2% of the global human population seemingly vanish without a trace. The show follows the stories of the devastated people left behind, from Justin Theroux’s troubled police officer Kevin to Christopher Eccleston’s unhinged religious zealot Reverend Matt Jamison.

Although the characters of The Leftovers gradually crossed paths throughout the HBO show’s story, the series wasn’t in a rush to reveal the links between its sprawling ensemble. With a starry cast that included Liv Tyler, Regina Hall, and Carrie Coon, The Leftovers wasn’t short on talent, but the show’s most divisive outing did leave viewers wondering whether its diffuse storytelling style would ever pay off.

The Leftovers season 1, episode 4, “BJ and the AC,” is often singled out as a rare miss for the show, and one of the only skippable episodes of the series as a whole. At the time of its release, some reviewers noted that episode 4 was left out of screeners for the HBO series, which can sometimes indicate that an episode isn’t likely to be particularly notable or memorable in the long run.

Compared to the preceding episode’s fascinating, focused character study, the plot of “BJ and the AC” felt shapeless and saggy. The subplot involving Jill and her friends didn’t capture believable teen dialogue particularly well, while The Leftovers was a little too on-the-nose in its religious symbolism when it came to the Nativity scene’s missing Baby Jesus doll. Even the very concept of the police assigning Kevin to search for a toy doll stretched credulity for some viewers.

However, especially when compared to controversial creator Damon Lindelof’s later Watchmen re-imagining from 2019, “BJ and the AC” is far from terrible. In fact, despite how heavy-handed its unsubtle symbolism is at times, the episode still finds time to make The Guilty Remnant a more authentically unsettling presence, while Kevin’s character flaws get more airtime in an outing that complicates his initial introduction.

As The Leftovers continued, characters like Jill were fleshed out further and the show outdid itself so many times that “BJ and the AC” started to look like a comparably messy, weak early effort. However, in comparison to many of the show’s competitors, this episode of The Leftovers is still an immersive, intriguing entry into the show’s larger story.

It is arguably unfortunate for the legacy of The Leftovers that HBO’s far shorter, dystopian, character-driven literary adaptation, Station Eleven, never released a single bad episode. However, The Leftovers lasted a lot longer and had many more episodes, so it is easy to forgive a few missteps from the typically stellar Mystery Box series.

#3395. Peacock’s 9-Episode Thriller Miniseries Is a Masterpiece Worth the Binge

Science fiction has advantages that few other genres possess. It can create fascinating worlds completely different from our own and use this removal of real-world contexts to explore fascinating issues surrounding free will and dystopian societies. From Paradise to The Handmaid's Tale, Black Mirror to The Running Man, the genre keeps on producing quality narratives that thoroughly entertain audiences with thought-provoking concepts. If you're looking for your next binge in this realm, there is no better place to look than Peacock's Brave New World miniseries.

The two worlds are separated by a blue barrier that only emphasizes the division in society. Rather than trying to help the Savage Lands, New London citizens view them as a lesser species, not understanding why they commit to monogamy or a more individualistic society. When the Savage Lands begin a rebellion focused on destroying New London, members on both sides of the conflict begin to doubt their own way of life. With sex being a key aspect of Brave New World (there are multiple orgy scenes), it examines whether sexual relations can be purely hedonistic and not lead to love and whether that love truly leads to peace, or just increases the chance of jealousy and strife.

On top of this, the societal hierarchy is given a recontextualizing in this world, as not only are children grown in a lab, but from conception, they are designated a status from Beta to Alpha Plus, which their heads-up displays constantly show next to everyone. This makes every interaction a focus on power dynamics, whether it is two alphas talking or a beta being rude to an alpha. Even the Savage Lands are presented through beautiful cinematography. While it is clear that it is desolate, the expansive nature of its desert and bright colors make the world feel full of passion and emotion, contrasting New London's overly clean and cold presentation.

From classics like Metropolis and Alien to Everything Everywhere All At Once, this is Collider's ranking of the best science fiction movies ever.

The mystery of what is known as an Epsilon, essentially a human worker-bee bred to do whatever they are told, killing themselves, is a fascinating subversion of the typical detective mystery. Bernard (Harry Lloyd) is the first on the scene and uses the technology of the world to see the worker's memories, giving him a personal attachment to the suicide that drives him to search for the truth. It is similar to I, Robot in how Brave New World can incorporate its sci-fi elements into not just the world-building, but the story and character arcs themselves.

Brave New World populates its incredible world with a wide range of characters who all question whether their society is the correct one. In New London, Lenina (Jessica Brown Findlay) and Bernard struggle with the enforced happiness and refusal of monogamy, yet their patronizing view of the Savage Lands makes them complex characters who know no better than to make fun of a way of life most viewers live themselves. In the Savage Lands, John (Alden Ehrenreich) and his mother, Linda (Demi Moore), feel stuck in the middle of the conflict, trying to better their lives in a world that has little place for good people.

This conflict makes Demi Moore's character particularly fascinating. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, Moore called her character, who is an Ex-New London citizen, a "bridge between the two worlds" as she dreams of her son leaving the Savage Lands for a better life in New London. Yet, her cold and even dismissive attitude toward John gives her a layered presentation of motherly love.

In the end, Brave New World is certainly worth the binge. With nine episodes and a myriad of twists and turns, Brave New World runs at a high pace that keeps the audience guessing where this terrible conflict will go next. There are few worlds as detailed and well-thought-out as Brave New World's, and the stacked cast keeps the audience engaged even in scenes where characters are merely exploring the world, whether that is listening to music from "before" or watching a pantomime-like performance of a conflict-filled marriage ceremony. While some scenes contain graphic sexual content that may make you want to look away, it's worth noting that every detail in Brave New World is intriguing and deserves your attention.

#3391. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

The Take streams on Netflix on Friday, January 15, 2027.

The streamer has started unveiling next year's releases, and The Take is one of two films releasing early in 2027. The other is Danny Boyle's INK, which debuts in theaters on December 11, 2026, before streaming on January 8, 2027. TV shows include The Twin (January 1), Jamie Dornan and MacKenzie Davis' crime thriller; Old Dog, New Tricks Season 2 (January 1), a Spanish dramedy; 3-Body Problem Season 2 (January 14), the hit sci-fi drama from Game of Thrones creators that is returning after three years; Grown Ups (January 14), a family drama costarring Robert Sheehan (Umbrella Academy); Blue Eye Samurai Season 2 (January 19), an animated series; Ginny & Georgia (Season 4) returns with more mother-daughter and YA drama; and The Palace of Secrets (January 22), a Spanish period romance drama starring Carlos Cuevas (Merli) and Carla Campra.

Stream The Take when it hits Netflix in January, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3387. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3382. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3380. James Bond Director’s Psychological Thriller Is Officially an Apple TV Streaming Smash

15 years ago, there weren’t many movie fans that had heard of Denis Villeneuve, but flash forward to today, and he’s one of the most prominent directors/writers in all of Hollywood. Villeneuve is a sci-fi savant who is widely known and celebrated for his work on Dune and Dune: Part Two, but his work with the sci-fi genre extends well beyond Arrakis’ reach.

Four years before the first Dune movie, Villeneuve took the reins from Ridley Scott for Blade Runner 2049, which is one of the most beloved sci-fi films of the 2000s despite its underwhelming box office performance. Villeneuve was already red-hot off the back of directing Arrival, the critically acclaimed sci-fi epic starring Amy Adams and Jeremy Renner. The year before Arrival, he directed Sicario, which was written by Taylor Sheridan.

Next up for Denis Villeneuve after Dune: Part Three releases in less than one month is the next James Bond movie, which is now confirmed to star Robert Pattinson as 007. Villeneuve will have to rely on his years of experience as a director to helm the best Bond film possible, calling on elements from all of his past movies, even Prisoners, the 2013 crime epic starring Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal.

Villeneuve spent $46 million on the making of Prisoners, but the film proved to be a worthy investment by grossing $122 million at the global box office — an impressive run for a director’s first American movie. 13 years after Prisoners left theaters, the film has finally found a streaming home on Apple TV, where it surged into the top 10 during the last week.

In addition to Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal, Prisoners also features other stars you’ll likely recognize, such as Viola Davis and Paul Dano. Aaron Guzikowski, who also wrote the Ridley Scott HBO Max sci-fi series, Raised by Wolves, penned the script for Prisoners. The official synopsis for Prisoners, which earned strong scores of 82% from critics and 87% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes, reads as follows:

“Keller Dover (Hugh Jackman) faces a parent's worst nightmare when his 6-year-old daughter, Anna, and her friend go missing. The only lead is an old motorhome that had been parked on their street. The head of the investigation, Detective Loki (Jake Gyllenhaal), arrests the driver (Paul Dano), but a lack of evidence forces Loki to release his only suspect. Dover, knowing that his daughter's life is at stake, decides that he has no choice but to take matters into his own hands.”

Check out Prisoners on Apple TV and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Denis Villeneuve’s future projects, like Dune: Part Three and the new James Bond movie.

#3379. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

#3374. Netflix’s Star-Studded WWII Movie Officially Arrives This Week

Like other streaming services nowadays, Netflix has started to warm up to releasing its films in theaters — at least some of them. The streaming service strongly considered leaning into this route when it tried to acquire Warner Bros., despite having the streaming-at-home line for the longest time. Some of its films this year have received limited theatrical runs in anticipation of Academy Award nominations, and the service has one strong contender so far: La Bola Negra. The Spanish epic has received acclaim from fans and critics, putting it in a strong position for awards in various categories.

Apart from La Bola Negra, Netflix has also given limited releases to The Further Misadventures of Cliff Booth, INK, Ray Gunn, and more. However, one of these films hasn't performed well critically, a telltale sign that its Oscar campaign has reached a natural end. That movie is a World War II epic that made its theatrical debut last month and has grossed $815813 across 349 theaters. Now, The Mosquito Bowl is coming to Netflix this week, and it could be a streaming hit.

Directed by Peter Berg and based on a script he co-wrote with Mark L. Smith, the action thriller is set in the 1940s and follows four American college football stars in the aftermath of the attack on Pearl Harbor. These young men abandon their promising careers to enlist as Marines in America's war with Japan. "As they prepare for the brutal invasion of Okinawa, they'll play in a legendary game featuring some of the greatest players in history — a game that, for many, will be the last they ever play," reads the film's description. Cast members include Nicholas Galitzine (John McLughry), Bill Skarsgård (Bob Bauman), Ray Nicholson (Tony Butkovich), and Tom Francis (Dave Schreiner). The Mosquito Bowl streams on Netflix on November 25.

With a current 41% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes, the film has not received the best reviews. Critics noted that The Mosquito Bowl feels quite hollow in more ways than one. Collider's Maggie Lovitt said that it is a bit pedestrian and "adds very little new to the canon of war epics," while ScreenRant's Lizzie Declan did not appreciate the violence used to shield the lack of an engaging story. RogerEbert's Robert Daniels said it is "lacking in humanity." However, critic reviews don't always reflect viewer consensus, and those who saw it in theaters gave it a favorable 91% rating. Netflix could be vindicated when The Mosquito Bowl finally enters friendlier territory.

Stream the film on Wednesday, November 25, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3372. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.
