The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

#3368. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3367. 7 Masterpiece Fantasy Book Series, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Starting a fantasy series is a big commitment. Some of the genre’s most beloved sagas run for thousands of pages, with maps, family trees, and made-up languages that can feel overwhelming before the story even begins. So many fantasy series get lost in endless exposition and keep bombarding readers with information before giving them a single reason to care.

By the time the story actually gets going, most people have already put the book down. However, a good fantasy series knows exactly how to strike the balance between building a rich world and telling a compelling story with characters that the readers instantly fall in love with. Here are the seven greatest fantasy book series of all time that can turn even the most casual of readers into lifelong enthusiasts of the genre.

Robert Jordan’s The Wheel of Time is one of the most expansive fantasy series ever written — one that rewards its readers’ commitment every step of the way. The story begins in a quiet farming village called the Two Rivers, where a mysterious woman named Moiraine arrives searching for someone. She belongs to the Aes Sedai, a powerful order of women who can channel magic. Moiraine believes that one of the village’s young men, possibly a humble shepherd named Rand al’Thor, is the Dragon Reborn: a legendary figure destined to face the Dark One. The problem is that the same prophecy says the Dragon could also break the world all over again.

The series spans 14 main novels, and its world is magnificent in scope, with dozens of nations and cultures that all feel distinct instead of ever blurring together. The story doesn’t leave a single loose thread and handles its big question of destiny with immense responsibility. Rand al’Thor has to carry the weight of a fate he never asked for, and since male magic-users in this world slowly go mad, his power is as much a curse as a gift. The middle books are famously slow, but the payoff is worth it in the end. Jordan passed away before he could finish the series, and author Brandon Sanderson completed the final three books using his notes. The Wheel of Time remains a towering achievement, with an ending that ties together 14 books’ worth of prophecies in a way that left longtime fans completely satisfied.

Brandon Sanderson is one of the most popular fantasy authors still writing today, and The Stormlight Archive is his magnum opus. The series is set on Roshar, a harsh world battered by massive storms so powerful that the plants and animals have evolved to survive them. Its heroes are a group of broken people. Kaladin is a former soldier sold into slavery, while Shallan is a young scholar hiding a dangerous secret. Dalinar is a battle-hardened warlord trying to make up for the terrible things he’s done. As an ancient threat returns, each of them is drawn toward the long-lost order of warrior-magicians known as the Knights Radiant.

For a plot so grand, The Stormlight Archive makes sure that it never takes away from the characters’ struggles. Kaladin’s fight with depression is one of the most honest portrayals of mental health in fantasy, and it grounds the world’s fantastical elements in something that plenty of readers can relate to. Sanderson is also famous for his carefully designed magic systems, which follow clear rules and make every battle feel like a clever puzzle. The books are complex, but they move fast, and each one builds to a huge climax that fans call a “Sanderlanche.” Five books in the series are out so far, with five more planned, which means the best may still be yet to come. The Stormlight Archive is the series modern fantasy fans can’t stop recommending, and for good reason.

Discworld proves that fantasy doesn’t have to take itself seriously to be brilliant. Terry Pratchett’s series is set on a flat world that rests on the backs of four elephants, which in turn stand on a giant turtle swimming through space. Over 41 novels, Pratchett fills this ridiculous world with unforgettable characters, including the bumbling wizard Rincewind and Commander Sam Vimes of the city watch. Death himself is a recurring character in the story, who speaks entirely in capital letters.

The genius of Discworld is that it starts as a fantasy parody and slowly turns into something much more meaningful. Pratchett uses his silly world to poke fun at politics, religion, and human nature, and his jokes often sneak up on readers with surprisingly moving ideas. The series also has a unique structure, since it is made up of several smaller storylines that can be read in almost any order, which makes it easy for newcomers to jump in at any given time. Pratchett was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s later in life but kept writing until he died in 2015. Discworld is funny and wise in equal measure, and it’s the most comforting series on this list.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Long before Game of Thrones took over TV, George R.R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire had already started reshaping the fantasy genre. The story is set in Westeros, where powerful noble families fight a brutal war for control of the Iron Throne. The Starks and Lannisters scheme and battle, while the exiled princess named Daenerys Targaryen is building an army across the sea. All of that is threatened by an ancient danger that is stirring in the frozen north. Of course, that is only half the story, and A Song of Ice and Fire covers a lot more ground, with storylines that converge and diverge all the time. Every chapter is told from a different character’s point of view, so readers see the war and power struggle from all sides.

The biggest shock of the series is how willing Martin is to break the rules. Characters who seem like the hero can die at any moment, and good people often make terrible choices. That realism made the books feel unpredictable in a way fantasy rarely had before. Martin also writes morally gray characters better than almost anyone, and some of the most hated figures in the early books slowly become fan favorites, which is a testament to the author’s brilliant storytelling. The big catch is that the series is still unfinished, with fans waiting more than a decade for the next book, The Winds of Winter. Even so, A Song of Ice and Fire is the series that made fantasy feel dangerous, and its influence is everywhere.

Decades before Hogwarts, Ursula K. Le Guin sent a young boy to wizard school. A Wizard of Earthsea follows Ged, a goatherd with a natural gift for magic who grows up on an island in a vast world made almost entirely of oceans and small archipelagos. The only problem is that Ged knows how good he is, and his pride often leads him right into dangerous situations. While he is still a student, Ged tries to prove himself by performing a forbidden spell and accidentally unleashes a terrifying shadow creature into the world. He spends the rest of the novel being hunted by it, until he finally has to turn around and face it.

What makes Earthsea special is how thoughtful yet simple it is compared to most fantasy books. In this world, magic works by knowing the true name of things, and every spell comes with a cost, so even the most powerful wizards are careful with their gifts. Le Guin was also ahead of her time in deliberately making most of her characters, including Ged, people of color. All the books in the series are short and beautifully written, and they explore big ideas like balance and death in a way that’s easy to follow. Earthsea has inspired countless writers, and it’s a must-read for anyone who wants to understand where modern fantasy came from.

Everyone knows about Harry Potter at this point, because it has become a permanent part of modern pop culture. J.K. Rowling’s seven-book series follows Harry, an orphan who discovers on his 11th birthday that he’s a wizard and has a place at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. There, he makes lifelong friends in Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, and he slowly learns the truth about the dark wizard Lord Voldemort, who killed his parents and has never stopped trying to kill him.

The reason why the Harry Potter series still resonates with the entire world is that it grows up with its readers. The first books are full of wonder and whimsy, but the series gets darker and more mature with every installment, until the final chapters cover a full-blown war. Rowling also had a gift for mystery, and each book is built around a central mystery that keeps readers guessing until the last chapter. The friendship between Harry, Ron, and Hermione is the heart of this fantastical story that readers just can’t get enough of. The series turned an entire generation into readers, and with a new HBO series on the way in December 2026, Harry Potter is not losing its magic anytime soon.

The Lord of the Rings is the series that has defined practically every other book on this list. J.R.R. Tolkien’s epic is often published as three volumes, but the author actually wrote it as a single story. Now, he obviously didn’t invent elves, dwarves, or epic quests, but he turned them into the blueprint the entire genre still follows. The story picks up years after The Hobbit, when a young hobbit named Frodo Baggins learns that the plain gold ring his uncle Bilbo left him is actually the One Ring, forged by the Dark Lord Sauron to control the world. The only way to stop Sauron is to carry the Ring into his kingdom of Mordor and throw it into the volcano where it was made. Frodo then sets out with a fellowship of companions, including the wizard Gandalf and his loyal friend Samwise Gamgee, as war spreads across Middle-earth.

What makes the series so powerful is that its real villain isn’t just Sauron, but the Ring itself, which slowly tempts and corrupts anyone who holds it. Tolkien fought in World War I, and his experience shows in the way the books treat war as something that leaves lasting scars. The world Tolkien creates feels extremely real. Middle-earth comes with its own languages and thousands of years of history. That depth gives The Lord of the Rings a sense of age and meaning like no other. Peter Jackson’s films brought the franchise to a new generation, but nothing comes close to the brilliance of the source material.

#3365. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

#3361. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

#3355. Apple announces App Store price changes in multiple countries, new California tax rules

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”

#3351. The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3349. Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest …

Whether there was or wasn't a cyber attack, I wouldn't believe a single word from the White House.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

#3346. MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

#3339. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3338. The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

Didn’t the iPhone 6 or the iPhone 11 already have a curved front glass?

Ice Universe says that two of the four models have quad-curved glass backs and two have flat glass. They indicate that Apple has already had to ramp back its ambitions with the curvature.

Apple is currently developing four models in total: two with flat glass backs and two with quad-curved glass backs. Apple has been prototyping this quad-curved design for three years, making several revisions along the way—particularly regarding the glass curvature, which is still being refined. The earliest version had a very pronounced curve; it was later reduced somewhat.

We’re expecting Apple to use a combination of ultra-thin bezels and curved glass to create the illusion of no bezels at all – a more sophisticated version of the effect seen on the Apple Watch. Today’s report says the bezels are around 1mm thick.

We yesterday saw an AI-generated render of what the design could look like. It’s expected to be the biggest redesign of the standard iPhone since the iPhone X.

#3335. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3331. New Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K just got a firmware update

Apple has released a firmware update for the new Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K, according to AppleDB. Here’s what you should know.

Last week the new Apple TV 4K officially launched, and with it an updated Siri Remote that adds a built-in speaker and Precision Finding so it’s harder to lose.

Although it’s rare for the Siri Remote to get firmware updates, Apple pushed out new firmware for the latest Siri Remote just yesterday per AppleDB.

You can’t manually update your Siri Remote’s firmware. But as long as it’s sufficiently charged and connected to your Apple TV, the update will install automatically in the background.

This update is only available for the new Siri Remote (4th gen).

If you’re interested in the new Siri Remote, but don’t want to buy a whole new Apple TV 4K, it’s available here as a $59 purchase and works with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models.

I haven’t personally encountered any issues with the latest Siri Remote since getting it last Friday, but apparently Apple discovered a problem that needed fixing.

Have you had any issued with the new Siri Remote? Let us know in the comments.

#3330. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#3329. Gustavo Dudamel Enlists Dave Grohl, LL Cool J, Cynthia Erivo for Brad Pitt-Produced Documentary

I n December, Gustavo Dudamel will make his much-anticipated return to conduct the Los Angeles Philharmonic for a string of dates. It’s the first time he will head back to his former home of nearly 20 years since beginning his tenure as the New York Philharmonic’s Music and Artistic Director. Given the multiple standing ovations and chants of “Gustavo” that resonated through the Hollywood Bowl during his final LA Phil bow in late August, his arrival will be a much welcome one.

Alongside his trip back to the West Coast, Rolling Stone can exclusively announce a documentary about Dudamel and the LA Phil will premiere on Dec. 7 coinciding with his concerts at Walt Disney Hall on Dec. 4, 5, and 6. The documentary, titled Symphony of a Thousand, is described as “Set during challenging times in L.A., the film encapsulates Dudamel’s philosophy on how music can create connection and community in an increasingly fractured world.”

The Jennifer Tiexiera-directed film, produced by Brad Pitt’s Plan B Entertainment, features footage from Dudamel and the LA Phil’s pair of performances at 2025’s Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, where they made history as the first major orchestra to perform a full set at the massive event. It features Dave Grohl,  LL Cool J, Cynthia Erivo, Natasha Bedingfield, Becky G, CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, and Zedd. Kevin Macdonald serves as the executive producer, with producers Jeremy Kleiner, Dede Gardner, and Chloe Mamelok.

Landmark pop culture moments like this have peppered the course of Dudamel’s trailblazing career. And he wasn’t about to go (east) quietly. His final nights helming the LA Phil culminated in a weekend at the Bowl that featured the Foo Fighters and other pop luminaries, concerts that doubled as a benefit for his home country of Venezuela. A conversation at the Grammy Museum followed.

“I met Gustavo at a party about 12 years ago, and I fell in love with him. As a heterosexual man, it confused me,” Coldplay’s Chris Martin affectionately jokes when joining Dudamel and LA Phil onstage during the benefit concert for Venezuela finale. “And I realized it wasn’t so much sexual as musical in the way I just wanted to cuddle him forever. And we’ve been musically cuddling ever since.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Trailing Dudamel during his final full-time week in L.A., that sentiment carries through to every interaction. At the closed final rehearsal on a Sunday morning in August, camera crews swirl around as two women busily work to notate the score, and a handful of onlookers from the team at the Bowl gather to take in the moment in the blazing heat. There’s a hushed reverence knowing an era is coming to an end, but also smiles abound, particularly from Dudamel who warmly hugs old friends as they join him onstage.

As he conducts, he throws the full weight of his body in a stance both graceful and animated — like a kid at his first dance. His baton alights in the air and comes down, and the orchestra responds, while he swoops and sways to the music. “5/4 pum pum,” Dudamel instructs as they run through one composition. Later, Meme del Real from Café Tacvba takes the stage to rehearse the poignant “Eras.” Lasso follows with an a cappella of “En Otra Vida.”

It’s the morning after their phenomenal performance with Foo Fighters, which marked the band’s first-ever set at the Hollywood Bowl. That pairing is not an unusual one for Dudamel, though. He’s made a name for himself breaking down perceived traditional genre boundaries in his 17 years at the Bowl, where he’s collaborated with an array of artists, including LL Cool J, Christina Aguilera, and Beck, who later at the finale concert performs “Ride Lonesome.” Beck’s dad, celebrated arranger-composer David Campbell, also attends the final rehearsal. Related Content Foo Fighters, Noah Kahan, the Who Lead New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival Lineup See Foo Fighters Return to ‘Baker Street’ on ‘Kimmel’ Foo Fighters Go Back to the Start on 'Kimmel' With 'This Is a Call' Foo Fighters Play ‘Window,’ Dave Grohl Talks Taylor Hawkins on ‘Kimmel’

“If I reflect about how I feel, yes, I feel exhausted,” Dudamel tells Rolling Stone with a smile when we meet at the Grammy Museum a couple of days later. “Every day a rehearsal, every day a concert. Next day a different program, another concert.” It’s been a nonstop whirlwind, but it’s also been a time “full of beauty,” he says.

“I have the chance to dive inside of all of that amount of talent — because it’s not only the soloists that play with me; it’s all that orchestra, that 100 musicians that are there, that I have shared 17 years of my life with them, and of course it doesn’t finish,” he continues. “This goes to eternity because when you develop something that is so deep and so powerful as developing an identity through music, it’s the biggest privilege … Every single note, every single second that I have the chance to share, or people share with me, that is a privilege to have the chance to work with all of these people and to create all of this environment.”

If there are a couple of overarching words to describe Dudamel, they would be magnetic charm. When we arrive at the Grammy Museum a few hours before his event, several people rush him to ask for selfies, to which he happily obliges before he’s quickly ushered into the building. People from the music world and beyond appear drawn to him, not only for the music he helms and the open environment he’s created around it, but also for his altruism.

At intermission during Dudamel’s Hollywood Bowl finale, Coldplay’s Martin heads backstage to rehearse with YOLA, the youth orchestra inspired by Dudamel’s own experience coming up in El Sistema, the publicly-funded National Network of Youth and Children Orchestras of Venezuela. (It was there while discovering music technique that “I saw the immense and infinite possibilities of all kinds of music,” Dudamel says.) Martin asks each child their name before leading them through a warm-up and taking to the piano. He vamps his lyrics to “Viva La Vida” before the choir comes in with the buoyant Oh-oh-oh bridge. “Absolutely fantastic,” Martin tells the students. He reminds them: “Remember when we’re out there onstage, this is our band … We’re doing this together.” Later onstage, they deliver their spine-tingly performance, which prompts a crowd-wide sing-along.

YOLA, which provides free instruments and education to create social change through music, is a vital part of Dudamel’s legacy and his north star. “I grew up not in an environment of conservatory, rigid. No,” he says. “It was music as a tool of social transformation — that is El Sistema. And of course, for me, opening spaces for young people to have access to music as a tool for them to have beauty, to have creativity, to have empathy, creating together — that is for me the most important thing. And [as] artistic institutions, we have to do that … for people to see the transforming power of music.

“When you have this chance to transform your life, creating harmony, creating beauty together — when you go out as a citizen, you behave differently because you see the real dimension of connection that goes beyond any material thing, any ideological point of view, and then you are connected through the empathy of human being and doing things beautiful for others.”

As for his hopes to bring a similar program to New York and beyond, he believes it’s imperative. “We don’t have the chance in this world to contemplate, to really see each other, to create something that requires discipline, but at the same time joy together. When you are doing music, in an orchestra, in a choir, and you feel that first moment that you create harmony and that you are part of something beautiful and powerful, that enhances your spirit. I think that is the way for our kids to be inspired, especially in the chaotic but beautiful, in the only world that we have. So we have to create more spaces like this.”

As a longtime champion of crossover collaborations, Dudamel attracts artists across genres and disciplines, but a recent team-up came by way of an unusual source, via actor Bradley Cooper, who is a mutual friend of Dudamel’s and Stella Hopkins. Hopkins began sharing scores with Dudamel, which were composed by her husband, actor Anthony Hopkins. It led to them working on an album.

“The thing about musicians is that they, unlike actors, they don’t have that ego,” Anthony Hopkins tells Rolling Stone of working with Dudamel. The pair met up at the Grammy Museum to talk about their collaboration on Hopkins’ debut classical album, Life Is a Dream. Dudamel conducted London’s Philharmonia Orchestra for the project, which comprises work Hopkins has composed over the course of more than six decades.

During his Venezuelan benefit show, Dudamel and LA Phil performed Hopkins’ “Stella Aria,” a moving ode to the actor’s wife, which featured a beautiful solo from Venezuelan cellist Gregorio Nieto at the concert.

“It is a great honor and a privilege because he actually endorsed my music,” says Hopkins. “I mean, I’m always filled with self-doubts as we all are … I have no theoretical, technical, musical training as such — everything is instinctive from childhood. So, naturally in me is the — ‘do I, is this good enough?,’ But when I sat there and Gustavo got up onto the podium to conduct the massive orchestra there, and I was astounded as the sound came out. He’s playing my music. Did I write that?’”

Dudamel has a knack for making artists feel comfortable in new situations as his next act in New York illustrates — it has begun, unsurprisingly, with rave reviews. In September, his premiere debut with the New York Philharmonic at Radio City Music Hall drew the kind of rock star lineup one would expect from Dudamel. Hosted by Liev Schreiber, it featured Lizzo, St. Vincent, and Joaquina. “The Philharmonic plays for Dudamel with visible investment and enthusiasm,” a New York Times review of his first week’s New York concerts reads. “Its members haven’t looked this happy onstage in years. Either he inspires them, or his starry arrival has lifted their morale. Or both. Whatever is going on, it works.” Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake

It’s apparent his inclusive approach to music uplifts both musicians and fans alike. And it is contagious. His Radio City Music Hall opener began with a standing ovation.

“That is one thing that I love the most. You know, to really make people see that there are no borders between us — we enjoy, we can be there, we can be listening,” he says of his approach. “When you really listen not only with your ears, but with your soul, the music becomes a dimension that is infinite.”
