#3251. Robert Eggers Is “Eager” To Move Away From Horror Genre: “I Think I Need A Break”

From witches to vampires and werewolves, Robert Eggers has had his fill of the horror genre after more than a decade.

The Werwulf co-writer and director recently explained that he’s ready to break free from “Robert Eggers’ House of Horror” as he hopes to explore other genres with his next project, following Werwulf‘s Christmas premiere in theaters.

“I’m eager not to continue purposely doing Robert Eggers’ House of Horror,” Eggers said during a recent Q&A. “I don’t need to do the Mummy or The Opera. Not to say that I won’t, but I think I need a break.”

Eggers’ comments come amid recent talks with Focus Features over an adaptation of William Shakespeare’s Romeo & Juliet, which he explained would be “a break” from the next horror pic he was planning. Watch on Deadline

“I was doing something else,” noted Eggers. “But what happened was, after Werwulf, I was writing another horror movie, and it got so dark again, and I was like, ‘I need a break. So, I’ll do something about two teenagers killing themselves.'”

Following his 2015 feature debut The Witch, Eggers has been praised as a new master of horror with films like The Lighthouse (2019), Nosferatu (2024) and Werwulf, premiering Dec. 25 from Focus Features.

In Werwulf, a man (Aaron Taylor-Johnson) in 14th century England finds him and his family threatened by a ravenous beast haunting the town. The film also stars Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe, Ralph Ineson and more.

#3250. iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms

Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri issues on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new issue you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496

It’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

How has Siri AI been working for you on HomeView? Let us know in the comments.

#3249. 10 Shows Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

Nearly 20 years later, Danny Ocean is trying to get the gang back together for Ocean’s 14, which was expected to begin filming in 2026.

David Leitch, who is attached to direct the fourth installment in the heist film franchise, recently noted that George Clooney and his Smokehouse producing partner Grant Heslov have delivered a “great script,” but scheduling issues stand in the way.

#3247. Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no plans for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Update: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:

“We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team plans. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”

#3245. ‘Madden’ Sparks Backlash From Raiders Owner Mark Davis Over Father Al Davis’ Portrayal: “That Hurts”

As John Madden‘s life gets the biopic treatment, his longtime colleague and friend Al Davis‘ family is not pleased with their late patriarch’s portrayal.

Las Vegas Raiders owner Mark Davis, whose father Al recruited Madden to coach for the NFL team when they were located in Oakland in 1967, criticized David O. Russell‘s Madden for its “totally unfair” depiction his father (portrayed by Christian Bale), who died at age 82 in 2011.

“It was full of turducken,” he told USA Today of the movie, referencing the Thanksgiving dish Madden popularized.

Mark continued, “As far as representations of my dad, yeah, that hurts, and I did the best I could to protect him. It’s absolutely a crime that they’re able to treat people that have passed away and characterize them in ways that are unfair, and there’s nobody around to protect their legacies. It’s just unfair. I don’t know what the purpose of the movie was to be real honest.” Watch on Deadline

He doesn’t consider his father “a pimp like Christian Bale played him, but that’s fine,” noting, “And I don’t blame Christian Bale. I don’t blame Nicolas Cage. All they did was what the director and the writers told them to do.”

Having screened the film two weeks before its release, Mark was surprised by a scene depicting the 1978 preseason game that paralyzed New England Patriots wide receiver Darryl Stingley, in which Al discourages Madden (Nicolas Cage) from seeing the player in the hospital.

“One of the main legacies of my father was how much he took care of people, whether it was on the Raiders or other teams,” said Mark. “People that were ill or needed help or whatever. He helped so many players on other teams that it’s incredible. And he did it quietly.

“And for them to put in the Darryl Stingley incident, that my dad was trying to talk John out of going to see him – that was just such a hurt to me personally, because that’s my father’s legacy, is how he treated people. No matter whether they were Raiders or not, he cared about people. That’s one of the redeeming qualities of my father throughout his life. And I just thought it was totally unfair for them to portray it that way,” added Mark.

While he said that scene “hurt” him, Mark added, “All the other crap, I could take all that (stuff). I don’t care if they talk about my haircuts and stuff like that. I don’t know what it had to do with anything, but I don’t mind that.  They can do that to me. But to do that to somebody that’s passed away, that can’t defend himself, is totally unfair. And I’m sure that there’s gonna be thousands of people that could contradict what that clip portrayed my father as.”

Mark added that the portrayal of his mother Carol Davis (played by Sienna Miller) and John’s wife Virginia Madden (Kathryn Hahn) is “all made up stuff too,” conceding, “But there are some, you know, elements of them in that. I will say that, but not much.”

Co-written by Russell and Cambron Clark, Madden charts John Madden’s career from Raiders coach to TV broadcaster to the namesake of the Madden NFL video game franchise.

#3243. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3242. If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

You obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

You can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

#3240. Halide camera app just got even better for iPhone Duo

Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide update also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

Lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Today’s new XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The update revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III launched back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

#3239. Todd Boehly Dissects How How Daniel Katz’s Trading Desk Acumen Fed Into A24 Success: “Very Few Entertainment People Understand Math”

Todd Boehly gave an insight into his no nonsense approach to investing in sports and entertainment in the concluding fireside chat of the Qatar Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days over the weekend.

The billionaire investor’s holding company Eldridge holds some $75B in assets including stakes in Backrooms distributor A24, and Fulwell Entertainment as well as the Los Angeles Lakers, the Los Angeles Sparks, the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Trent Rockets among many more.

The holding is also a partner with Deadline owner Penske Media in the Penske Media Eldridge unit encompassing live TV entertainment specialist Dick Clark Productions as well as events such as the Golden Globes and SXSW. Related Stories News Joe Russo Talks 'Doomsday' Teaser-Trailer Strategy Ahead Of Rumored Monday Drop: "I Have To interact With Fans" News Watermelon Expands Production Ambitions As It Seals Partnership With Qatar's Film Committee

Boehly first connected with A24 cofounder Daniel Katz, when the latter headed Guggenheim Partners’ film finance group in New York, while he was president of the global investment firm before leaving to create Eldridge. Watch on Deadline

“One of the things I believe is that there’s very few entertainment people that understand math… the math of entertainment is really about understanding how are you taking risk and then how are you distributing risk,” he said in the chat entitled “Playing to Win”.

“It’s no different than any other industry, if you’re thinking about what amount of risk you are willing to take and then how are you going to feed that risk,” he added.

Boehly said Katz had impressed him from the start for his ability to identify and work with risk during his time with Guggenheim Partners.

“Daniel’s real magic, when he worked on our trading floor from, let’s call it like 2008 to 2012, he didn’t take a lot of risks, but he said ‘no’ a lot,” he said.

“There was a slate that was done by a group called Stark Investments, and one of their big films was Poseidon. I remember it showed up on our desk. And Daniel was immediately like, this is a disaster. It’s going to cost so much money, you know, they’re not going to be able to make any return on it.”

The $160M disaster movie by Wolfgang Petersen went down in film financing folklore after it faltered at the box office and failed to gross enough to cover its P&A costs.

Boehly provided $19M in seed money for A24 as Katz launched the company in 2012 with David Fenkel and Joh Hodges. It was last publicly valued at $3.5 billion in June 2024.

“Everyone told me in Hollywood that there’s no room for another distribution company,” recalled the businessman. “His early successes with Spring Breakers and The Bling Ring were really structured finance trades.”

“You’re not really allowed to talk about that in the entertainment world because everything’s creative and creator driven… what Daniel was really good at, because he sat on a trading desk and he understood risk and he understood math, he was really good at figuring out how am I going to get my money back using different windows.”

Starring James Franco, Selena Gomez, Vanessa Hudgens, Harmony Korine’s Spring Breakers premiered in competition in Venice and went on to gross $31M.

“Spring Breakers cost a couple million bucks to buy, and he ended up making 10 million bucks or so very quickly on, because he really understood that it’s a structured finance straight,” said Boehly.

He added that beyond Katz’s business savviness, the company had also understood how to tap into social media to generate audience engagement as well as how to plug into trends of the moment.

“One of the things that A24 has done an amazing job at is being able to read the cultural zeitgeist. I think Civil War was really well timed; Marty Supreme was very well timed with Timothée Chalamet and his ascension as probably one of the top actors for the next couple of decades.”

Boehly also highlighted A24’s strategy of growing a cohort of directors and actors, who returned to work with the company on a regular basis.

“He wants repeat customers. He wants the directors coming back… he wants the actors coming back… because then it’s not a transaction, it becomes a recurring business with enterprise,” said Boehly.

“So many people think about the film business, ‘Oh, it’s a transaction’. But if you’re really thinking about how to build an enterprise, then you need to make sure that you have a recurring revenue base. And the way you do that in this industry is you get repeat users.”

He also gave insight into how Katz constructs A24’s slate in a way that enables it to work with established names and newcomers and turn a profit, suggesting that over a portfolio of 15 films, nine would be “the core bread and butter”.

“It’s a budget of 25 to 40 million bucks. It’s the expectation that he’s going to make 1.35 times,” he explained. “And if you think about the math of it again, you get 0.8 times your money back right away or very quickly. So, when you think about the risk that you have, you’re in for 0.2. If you make 1.35 and your risk capital is 0.2, but you’re going to make six, seven times that 0.2.”

“And then he’ll take three big swings and make something that has the capacity to become multiple films out of the content… he’ll take 1.2 times. So, he’ll modify his expectations on the rate of return to achieve something that might have more enterprise value or longevity on the back of it.”

Boehly suggested the final three films would be by up-and-coming young directors, and would require time, energy and effort rather than big financial investments and risk.

“He’s always thinking about how do I build that portfolio in order to have my bread and butter, have the opportunity to have something that’s got longevity and then find someone who’s going to be special in the industry,” he said.

#3238. How to Set Up Alexa Wishlist Alerts for Black Friday and Cyber Monday

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

Then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

If Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale."

Alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

#3237. iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a convenient new setting, here’s how to use it

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

One of the year's most anticipated sports films has finally landed on Prime, delivering a biopic football fans have long awaited: a profile of gridiron great John Madden. Nicolas Cage plays the titular icon who not only brought wins to the field, but also conquered the broadcast booth and the gaming sector by helping launch the blockbuster video game franchise of the same name.

Written and directed by David O. Russell, "Madden" spans an impressive career that saw the outspoken coach lead the Oakland Raiders to an unlikely Super Bowl win under new team owner Al Davis. The film also spotlights his legendary broadcasting run — where his infectious enthusiasm gave fans a masterclass in football’s strategic decisions — alongside his partnership with EA Sports founder Trip Hawkins to create the sports game to emulate.

While "Madden" arrives after a drought of memorable sports biopics, we once enjoyed decades of exquisitely filmed profiles of real-life icons. Whether they toiled on the diamond or battled for recognition on the gridiron, these legends inspired us with their courage, tenacity, and business smarts. If you’re looking to tap into your inner jock with remarkable stories you’ll long remember, check out the top five sports biopics you can stream right now.

If you haven’t seen Robert De Niro’s Oscar-winning turn as 1940s boxing champ Jake LaMotta in "Raging Bull," stop what you’re doing and watch this beaut of a film. Martin Scorsese’s powerhouse drama tracks LaMotta from a hungry middleweight amateur to a ferocious fighter feared across the country.

While his personal life imploded from unrelenting jealousy and rage, the boxing scenes are where sports fans will find the real magic. The visceral sound design and the cinematographer’s eye for putting us right inside the ropes remain just as stunning today as when the film dropped in 1980.

Football has its share of rewatchable classics, from "Friday Night Lights" to "Any Given Sunday," but "Rudy" stands out for anyone who knows the struggle of being told you aren't athletic enough to get a shot. The 1993 favorite introduces us to Daniel "Rudy" Ruettiger (poignantly played by Sean Astin), a plucky blue-collar kid from Joliet, Illinois, who dreams of suiting up for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

At 5-foot-6 and barely 160 pounds, he’s an underdog in every sense, and the road to glory is paved with painful stones. Even after making it onto campus, trying out for the squad brings relentless bullying and bruised pride, yet his work ethic never wavers. When he finally earns his spot on the roster, we’re left with a heartwarming reminder from the real Ruettiger: you’re never too small to make a difference.

A rare biopic focused on a front-office executive, "Moneyball" is astonishing on multiple levels. Based on the bestseller of the same name, this 2011 hit follows Oakland Athletics general manager Billy Beane (Brad Pitt), who teams up with a nerdy stats genius (Jonah Hill) to rebuild a roster gutted by the loss of star players. Instead of chasing pricey sluggers, they recruit strictly on underappreciated metrics like on-base percentage.

The story hooks you even if you aren't a die-hard MLB fan, shining a light on the statisticians and math aficionados who rescued managers stuck in 1980s-era habits of buying big names. "Moneyball" lingers long after the credits roll thanks to Aaron Sorkin’s razor-sharp screenplay, which crackles just as intensely during tense boardroom negotiations as it does out on the diamond. In our AI-driven, stats-hungry era, it holds up effortlessly.

Chadwick Boseman shone in "Black Panther," but his commanding turn as Jackie Robinson in "42" deserves every ounce of applause. Focusing on the mental resilience baseball’s first Black player had to forge amid rampant racism, the 2013 drama is a poignant portrait of both a generational talent and a cultural hero.

Even as his own teammates hurled insults to his face, Robinson forced the wider baseball community to judge players on their merits rather than the color of their skin. The film’s message lands so powerfully because it shows rather than tells, skipping didactic lectures and letting the tension breathe. We’re given space to reflect on Robinson’s massive impact while marveling at his rare gifts on the field, making it the kind of movie you want to revisit every few years to see how sports can open doors it once slammed shut.

In 2023, we were treated to a rare twist on the genre: a sports biopic where the star athlete never appears on screen. Neither Michael Jordan nor his likeness ever shows up in "Air," directed by and starring Ben Affleck—and yet the film completely works. Set in 1984, it follows Nike CEO Phil Knight (Affleck) as he tasks talent scout Sonny Vaccaro (Matt Damon) and marketing exec Howard White (Chris Tucker) with landing a young rookie on a shoestring budget.

Most of us see a pair of Jordans without realizing MJ still earns a cut of every sneaker sold today, all thanks to savvy deal-making and a sharp mother. In a tight 110 minutes, "Air" reveals what makes a custom shoe design pop—and how the Nike-Jordan agreement sparked the modern era of athlete equity partnerships. Along the way, Viola Davis steals the show as Jordan’s mother, blending sharp business acumen with a fierce commitment to securing her son’s legacy.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

According to a new report from Bloomberg, Apple’s head of camera and photo software retired last month. Jon McCormack spent eight years at Apple and “oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how users capture, view, and edit their pictures and video.”

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Mark Gurman reports that Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to replace McCormack, who reported to software chief Craig Federighi. “Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under other executives,” the report says.

In his role, McCormack oversaw “close coordination between software engineers and Apple’s camera hardware and chip teams.” He’s credited with last year’s redesigned selfie camera and other projects:

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year. This year, Apple added a variable-aperture camera to the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, giving users more control over lighting and depth of field. Bloomberg describes McCormack as a “strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photographs,” a philosophy that created tension as Apple embraced AI tools in the Photos app. His retirement, however, “wasn’t related to a disagreement or clash with Apple over its AI strategy,” the report says.

McCormack spoke in depth about iOS 27 features like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing in an interview with Tyler Stalman in June. He emphasized how the features “preserve the integrity of the moment.”

#3231. The Best Amazon Prime Benefits You Probably Don't Know About

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the company is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

If your lawn is buried under a blanket of fallen leaves like mine, raking them up has likely turned a routine chore into a real slog. When wet conditions set in, clearing leaves off the grass often turns into a time-consuming hassle.

And while my go-to steel rake has been my lifesaver, I often worry I might be causing damage to my healthy lawn in the process. This is especially the case when the leaves all clump together, making it a challenge to leave my grass spotless and debris-free.

I called on an expert to shed light on this and offer top tips on how to rake wet leaves without pulling up blades of grass. So before you get out to tackle your leaves on your lawn, here are expert-approved tips this season.

With wet weather making lawn care challenging, is raking damp leaves actually safe for my grass? “Yes, although wet leaves are heavier, stick together, and can be much more difficult to rake, blow, or vacuum,” states Karen Musgrave, Horticulturalist at Hicks Nurseries.

“The bigger concern for your lawn is allowing a thick layer of leaves to remain there for an extended period of time. A heavy mat of wet leaves can block sunlight and air from reaching the grass and trap excess moisture underneath.”

A heavy mat of wet leaves can block sunlight and air from reaching the grass and trap excess moisture underneath

In addition, leaving wet leaves sitting on your lawn over time can smother the grass, blocking essential nutrients from reaching the roots and making it prone to mold and fungal diseases. This can lead to patchy or thinning grass that will need urgent repair come springtime.

So what is the correct way to rake wet leaves without pulling up grass and harming my lawn? Experts agree that choosing the right tools is essential to do the job — and keep your yard intact.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

“If the lawn is wet, avoid being overly aggressive with a rake because you can pull at the grass,” advises Musgrave. “ For the lawn, I would choose a lightweight leaf rake with a wide head rather than a heavier garden rake.

“It gives you more control around garden beds, shrubs, and other areas where you don’t necessarily want to blow everything around. A smaller or narrower rake is especially helpful for removing leaves that have collected between plants in the landscape without damaging them.”

It’s also important to invest in a good-quality rake; aluminum or plastic rakes are best for most leaf cleanups. Unlike leaf blowers, a durable rake is affordable, easy, and practical to use, and doesn’t need fuel or batteries.

If in doubt, though, check out these different types of rakes suitable for your yard. For more top tips, check out how to rake leaves the easy way — 7 tips and tricks.

A top tip is to (ideally) rake on a dry day, as the leaves will be easier to gather and less of a chore.

Also, you don’t have to clear every single leaf off your lawn, since keeping a few around can actually benefit your garden plants. “Don’t blow or rake every leaf out of your garden beds just for the sake of making them spotless,” adds Musgrave.

“Some leaf litter can be beneficial for the soil as it breaks down and adds organic matter. It can also provide overwintering habitat for beneficial insects. You don’t want leaves piled so heavily that they smother smaller plants, but a light layer can be left in place.”

Shredding leaves with a lawn mower is another handy trick. Breaking them down into smaller pieces makes it easy to add them to your compost heap and return those valuable nutrients to your yard.

“Excess leaves can also be added to a compost pile rather than bagged and thrown away. Chopping or shredding them first can help them break down more quickly. The key is to make sure the leaves aren’t so thick they cover the grass and block sunlight and air.”

Finally, pay attention to bare spots and thin areas. Depending on your grass type and climate, consider overseeding before the harsh winter arrives. “Apply a grass seed that is appropriate for your lawn, lightly rake it into the soil, and keep the area consistently moist while the new grass gets established.

"The cooler temperatures of fall are ideal for establishing grass. Taking care of thin and bare spots now gives new grass time to develop roots before winter and helps create a fuller, healthier lawn for spring.”

Here’s when to plant grass seed in November to get the best results.

This Greenworks leaf blower delivers 770cfm/180mph of power with a runtime of 60 minutes, and a rapid recharge of one hour. It offers a variable-speed trigger, as well as cruise control for precision cleaning, so you can swap between heavy and light cleanups.

#3228. These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.)

#3227. Gemini app for Mac adds computer use to control desktop apps

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see new “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

#3226. ‘Cameron Winter’ Shines In Vibrant Indie Weekend, ‘Elsinore’ Opens Strong — Specialty Box Office

Andrew Scott-starring Elsinore is off to a nice start with a $240k limited opening on 6 screens in NY and LA. That’s a $40k per theater average as excellent exits polls bode well for the Focus Features’ film as it expands to 120 screens in top 25 markets starting Wednesday.

The true story of Ian Charleson, a gifted actor facing his own mortality with honesty, wit, and grace is “inspiring, and we could all use a movie that shows how you can live your life to the fullest even when you have obstacles in the way,” says Focus distribution chief Lisa Bunnell of the film, which has a 92% positive rating and an 80% recommend. Related Stories News 'Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' $120M U.S. Opening Is Second Best Start For A Prequel After 'Rogue One'; Lionsgate Franchise Returns To Fortune - Sunday Update News Indie Holiday Push: 'Minotaur', 'Elsinore' & 'Josephine' Debut With Cameron Winter Concert Film; 'Club Kid' Expands - Specialty Preview

Directed by Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, it world premiered at Telluride taking the International People’s Choice Award, followed by a winning festival run and lively screening program through Focus Insider, a community of 2 million. This is a meaningful project for Scott, who has been very actively promoting the film and the story behind it. Watch on Deadline

The film enters a crowded and dynamic period for the indie box office with a weekend of diverse debuts including a standout by Janus Films and Criterion’s exclusive 35mm tour of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter At Carnegie Hall. The concert film grossed $162k at just three locations for a $54k per-screen average, one of the year’s best. Shows were sold out at all theaters weeks in advance, and the 35mm-only meant additional showings couldn’t be added.

The tour continues through January, bringing the film to sixty of the largest historic theaters across the country for limited engagements, dozens of which have been sold out since October when the film premiered at the New York Film Festival. Theaters are selling exclusive merch at the shows. Up next is the Music Box in Chicago, The Castro in San Francisco, the AFI Silver Theatre outside Washington, D.C., and the TIFF Bell Lightbox.

God With Us, an event release from Variance Films in partnership with Blue Harbor Entertainment, saw a sizable $885k on 432 screens. The gross from writer-director Jimmy Jenkins’ modern day parable came largely without planned Saturday or Sunday evening showtimes, although theaters were adding them throughout the weekend. Originally programmed as a one weekend, three showtime event engagement, it will now remain in theaters throughout the holiday season.

Meanwhile, Club Kid from A24 grossed $1.4 million on 229 screens in limited release for a cume of $3.39 million. Jordan Firstman’s feature debut, with strong exits and word of mouth, continues to build ahead of a moderate nationwide expansion over Thanksgiving.

The distributor’s You Can See Everything remains in the top 10 (no. 6) after six weeks of release with a $2.5 million gross and a domestic cume of $93.4 million. The blockbuster doc by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim has crossed $100 million globally.

Limited: Neon’s Paper Tiger from James Gray grossed $336k in a week 2 expansion to 28 screens for a domestic cume of $622k. Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller star.

Mubi’s release of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, winner of the Cannes Grand Prix, opened to $97k at 3 theaters in New York and Los Angeles to a $32.4k PTA — the highest for two-time Oscar-nominated director. The Hitchcockian thriller saw several sold out shows across the weekend at all three opening theaters in a crowded specialty marketplace heading into the Thanksgiving holiday.

Josephine from Sumerian Pictures, winner of the Grand Jury and Audience Awards in U.S. Dramatic Competition at Sundance, debuted to $84.2k on 4 screens in New York and Los Angeles. Will hold in limited release through the Thanksgiving holiday weekend before expanding nationwide Dec. 4. “We couldn’t be prouder of the initial response to Beth de Araújo’s visionary work, or more excited to share it nationally with moviegoers on the crest of such positive word of mouth,” said Sumerian President Rob Williams.

Pedro Almodovar’s Bitter Christmas from Sony Pictures Classics is eyeing $44k in week 2 at 11 locations for a cume of $99k.

Ash and Crayons from Briarcliff Entertainment opened one NYC screen, Angelika’s Village East, to $11.5k. The documentary by Evgeny Afineevsky follows the lives of seven Ukrainian children swept into the war with Russia. With no previews or advance shows, three Q&A screenings with the director and producer Kevin Goetz sold out and other screenings played at or near capacity. Bohdan Yermokhin, one of the film’s subjects, traveled from Ukraine for the Friday premiere. Expand to additional screens and markets in the coming weeks.

Wide: Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky from Amazon MGM starring Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone had a solid expansion with $9.3 million on 2,448 screens in week 3 for a $10.4 million gross. Exit data is super with an A+ Cinema Score, 97% in the top two boxes; 88% def recommend.

Godzilla Minus Zero from GKids is pushing $$2.7 million on 2,107 screens for the weekend in the no. 5 spot with a cume of $54.5 million in week 3.

Searchlight Pictures’ Wild Horse Nine is no. 7 in week 3 on 2,000 screens with a $2.5 million gross and a circa $18 million cume.

Fathom’s release of Laika’s animated Wildwood is hanging in at no. 9 on 1,341 screens with $2 million for a $28.4 million cume.

Indian films are out in force. As Ramayana: Rise Of A Legend from Sony Pictures (distributing the Prime Focus Studios film) becomes the highest-grossing Indian film of all time at the domestic box office, rounding out the top ten, another trio of Indian films is adding heft to the domestic box office. ENE Repeat from Prathyangira Cinemas booked $698k from 385 screens for a cume of $1.26 million; OM: Operation Mole from Prime Media Pictures debuted to $532k at 260 locations; and Aakasamlo Oka Tara from Sarigama Cinemas is at $408.5k with 200 locations (all three as per Rentrak).

Ramayana hit $28.4 million through Sunday with a weekend gross of just over $2 million at 681 theaters.
